The fix works by that same inheritance into the li's <strong>. validated_work_order.approach:
Two files. One declaration in the stylesheet, and one abstraction in the test file that every stylesheet pin in it then uses, so that at the end of this change there is no second CSS parser left in the suite, plus the repair that makes the suite green so any of it can be verified. The diagnosis is settled and this round does not reopen it. What changes this round is four clauses a critique caught and one I caught reading the pin those clauses describe. R1 — ONE RULE ABOUT THE TERMINATING SEMICOLON, STATED ONCE. declarations(body, prop) treats a trailing chunk after the last ';' as a declaration, and every pin that reads through it therefore stays GREEN when a declaration loses its terminator. It is a STATED LOOSENING, stated in one place (AC-6(v)) and quoted nowhere except where a mutation is derived from it. M9 (the ';' off .page-title's line-height: 1.25) and M10 (the ';' off #main > *'s min-width: 0) are both GREEN. What guards #main > *'s terminator afterwards is nothing, and out_of_scope says so in those words with the CSS rule that makes it correct — a declaration's terminating ';' is optional when it is the last one in a block, so .page-title { margin: 0; line-height: 1.25 } and the same rule with the semicolon are identical to every browser. A pin that reddens on the difference is a pin on punctuation rather than on the property it exists to protect, which is the defect class this ticket was filed about. R2 — .page-title READS THROUGH declarations(), AND CARRIES ITS NON-EMPTY GUARD ACROSS. Today the pin is const rule = /\.page-title\s*\{([^}]*)\}/.exec(css) plus assert.ok(rule, 'src/web/styles.css defines a .page-title rule') plus three assert.match(rule[1], /prop:\s*value\s*;/) calls — first-match only, terminator-required. After this change it collects every NON-NESTED rule whose comma-split selector part is exactly .page-title, and that collection is asserted NON-EMPTY with the SAME message, before anything is asserted about its declarations. This clause is new and it is not optional. I measured the loss: deleting the .page-title rule from the stylesheet today reads 70 pass / 2 fail with test 65 red, and that redness comes from the assert.ok. forEach over an empty collection is vacuously true, so a migration that drops the guard turns the suite GREEN on a stylesheet with no .page-title rule at all — a deleted rule, the exact inverse of a second rule being appended. The strictness that is a real gain is preserved and is what M13 covers: appending .page-title { margin: 4rem; } is green under first-match and breaks the page, and under the every-match form it is red. R3 — THE SIX EXISTING PINS KEEP NESTED RULES IN THEIR MIGRATED COLLECTIONS. This is the correction that costs the most if an implementer gets it wrong. Today all six collect their rules with [...css.matchAll(/\s*\{([^}]*)\}/g)], which matches a rule wherever it sits, including inside an @media block. The coverage is live rather than theoretical, and it was measured on this tree rather than inherited: appending @media (max-width: 900px) { .table-scroll { overflow-x: visible; } } to src/web/styles.css makes node --test test/web/pages.test.js read 70 pass / 2 fail, the extra failure being test 66, and the file was afterwards restored byte-identically. An implementer who applies the new pin's non-nested filter to the six as well — the natural reading of 'one reader, one rule' — silently deletes six live nested-override checks and the suite goes green on exactly the defect this ticket exists to close. So: the six keep EVERY rule, top-level or nested, that matches their selector; the non-nested filter belongs to the new .awaiting-list pin alone. M12 pins it and is the one row a single implementer command settles. R4 — THE REPAIR FOR THE PRE-EXISTING RED USES THE FILE'S OWN IDIOM. Replace /
  • / with the token test the card pin already uses fifteen lines below it: extract the class attribute, split it on whitespace, assert the resulting Set contains approval-card, and separately assert the element carries data-testid="approval-card" per .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md. The regex /]*\bclass="[^"]*\bapproval-card\b[^"]*"/ is NOT used: \b after approval-card matches at a hyphen boundary, so it accepts
  • and
  • where the form it replaces rejects both. That is a new false negative on the rename axis #71 finding 2 was filed about, in the file that documents the lesson, and the token form is immune to it while still matching the shipped markup. R5 — THE #main:focus PAIR GETS A STATED COLLECTION POLICY EACH, because v12 mandated migrating these two pins and stated no policy for either, and the two candidate readings fail in opposite directions. The 345 pin collects every rule whose comma-split selector part is exactly #main:focus AND that is NOT nested, requires the collection NON-EMPTY, and asserts declarations(body, 'outline') deepEqual ['none'] on each. TOP LEVEL ONLY, and the reason is the file, not taste: the stylesheet has two such rules — one at top level with outline: none and one nested inside the @media (forced-colors: active) block with outline: 2px solid CanvasText — and the other test in the pair owns the second one at a different value. Collecting both and asserting none on each false-reds the shipped file, which is the one thing a migration must not do. A second TOP-LEVEL #main:focus rule is red here (M20), which is a verdict a first-match reader also misses. The 359 pin collects every NESTED rule whose selector part is exactly #main:focus, requires it non-empty, asserts declarations(body, 'outline') deepEqual ['2px solid CanvasText'] on EACH, and compares the two rules' SOURCE INDICES rather than the character offsets the file uses today. This is strictly stronger than the assertion it replaces and it is what closes the first-match blind spot: the pin today is /#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/.exec(css) with no g, so @media (max-width: 900px) { #main:focus { outline: auto; } } appended to the stylesheet is invisible to it and the suite stays green. Under R5 that mutation is red (M19). It keeps the length > 0 guard on the not-at-top-level lookup, so a reader regression that stopped descending into at-rules cannot make the test pass vacuously on a file with no carve-out at all, and it RE-SOURCES the bareRuleAt !== -1 guard from the reader rather than leaving it on raw text, where it silently changes meaning once the comment strip is in play — the stylesheet mentions #main:focus in prose in the comment above the rule. One consequence to state because it moved: the forced-colors pin's OLD regex only found the carve-out when it was the first thing in the block, so the reader's rewrite is strictly MORE PERMISSIVE and M18 is GREEN on purpose. 'Another nested rule before the carve-out' now means a rule with a DIFFERENT selector — a second #main:focus rule in the block is RED under the per-rule value assertion, which is the correct verdict, and it is stated so the row cannot be read two ways. R6 — THE DESCENDANT LIST IS A WATCH LIST, NOT AN ALLOW LIST, AND SAYS SO. AC-8(d) passes ['.awaiting-list', '.awaiting-list li', '.awaiting-list li strong', '.awaiting-list li span'] to conflictingOverrides, which reports any rule outside the pinned set declaring the property on any of them at any index. The consequence is that a CORRECT fix authored one level down — .awaiting-list li span { overflow-wrap: anywhere; }, the same inherited fix M6 accepts when it is placed on the parent — joins no collection and is reported as a conflict. That verdict is defensible: the pin is anchored on the li, the collection is the thing the fix must join, and a descendant-level declaration is a different edit from the one the stylesheet's own comment describes. What was not defensible is having neither a policy nor a matrix row for it, so the test's own comment now says the descendant entries are a WATCH list — a correct descendant-level fix is conservatively reported — and M6b names that verdict. Nothing is dropped from the list: dropping strong and span would turn the check into a same-selector check only, which is what the pin's own collection predicate already does. A. Add overflow-wrap: anywhere; to the EXISTING .awaiting-list li rule in src/web/styles.css, in place among its display / gap / border / border-radius / padding declarations, with a comment above the rule giving the wrap rule's reason the way the one above the four-card rule does. The comment is constrained by CONTENT and not by wording: it must give (a) that a grid item's automatic minimum is its min-content width, (b) anywhere rather than break-word, and (c) that the declaration reaches the by inheritance. It MAY or MAY NOT name the property in prose, and MUST NOT be written to any length. The plan previously constrained the comment's VOICE and then asserted a number the voice's wording decided; the two must not both happen, and every number in this order that depends on the comment's wording has been deleted rather than recomputed. No second rule with the same selector RE-DECLARES the property: the new pin collects every non-nested rule on that selector whose body declares the property and asserts the value on each, so such a rule joins the collection and reads RED against the VALUE assertion (M3a) — that is the mechanism, and it is NOT conflictingOverrides, which exempts the whole collected set by design and can never report a rule that joined it. A second rule on the same selector that leaves overflow-wrap alone is not collected and is GREEN (M3b), which is correct: a rule that neither declares overflow-wrap nor uses the all shorthand cannot change that property's computed value. The all bound is not decoration — .awaiting-list li { all: revert; } declares no overflow-wrap, so the collection and the conflict helper both skip it, and all resets the property to its initial value and reinstates the overflow with a green suite. The stylesheet already uses a * rule, so the shorthand is in house style. The bound is recorded in out_of_scope rather than pinned. B. Add four shared helpers near the top of test/web/pages.test.js, beside H1_HOOK and mainOf, and route all eight stylesheet read sites through them. readStylesheet() — the single readFileSync of src/web/styles.css, returning the SOURCE STRING. Every one of the eight sites becomes const css = readStylesheet();, the shape they have today, and the parse is one call on top. It returns the string rather than the parsed rules on purpose: the length > 0 guards and failure messages in those eight tests are about the FILE. Line 1611's readFileSync is NOT migrated: it reads test/web/pages.test.js itself inside the H1_HOOK call-site pin. cssRules(source) — strip /* */ with the SAME expression the card pin uses today (css.replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, ' ')), then walk with a brace stack. A frame whose selector starts with '@' is a BLOCK whose children are rules; any other frame is a rule whose body is declarations. ';' terminates a declaration inside a rule and a prelude inside an at-rule. Nested rules are emitted with their own selector and a nested flag meaning 'not at top level'. At-rule frames are not emitted. Every rule carries a source index. ONE EXCEPTION, and it is in the shipped file today: a block whose prelude is @keyframes (or @-webkit-keyframes) contains KEYFRAME STEPS, not style rules — skip its children entirely rather than emitting 0% / 100% as rules. A 0% selector matches nothing on a comma-split === comparison, so the mis-emission is harmless to every pin today, but it puts junk into the one structure every other helper depends on. TWO OTHER FAILURE MODES PRODUCE PLAUSIBLE OUTPUT AND NEITHER SHOWS UP UNTIL A PIN DEPENDS ON IT: accumulating the prelude through a rule body concatenates the last declaration onto the selector of the next nested rule (M16), and a reader that appends nested text to the parent body instead of descending into it drops every nested rule and reinstates the at-rule blind spot exactly (M11) — M11 is green under that second bug while every test in the file as written today still passes. This order pins NO rule count: a total breaks on every future stylesheet edit for no semantic reason and would not have caught either. declarations(body, prop) — one property's values from an already comment-stripped body, anchored on a declaration boundary (start of body, or after a ';') rather than a bare substring, with a trailing chunk after the last ';' treated as a declaration. THE REASONS FOR THE ANCHORING ARE MEASURED, and one commonly cited reason is false: 'min-width' is NOT a substring of 'min-height'. The reasons that are real, both green today: (a) a rule with no min-width at all but a comment naming one reads as a single value and the pin passes — the BUG-1 state passing the BUG-1 pin, because the min-width pin does not strip comments while the card pin beside it does; (b) a comment standing beside a real declaration is consumed as the declaration, so the widths come back as two values where the real floor is one. The third thing the boundary buys is the custom-property case: a bare substring search matches --min-width: 16ch and a boundary-anchored one does not, in a stylesheet whose :root declares seventeen custom properties. The trailing-chunk clause is R1 and nothing else. conflictingOverrides(rules, pinned, selectors, prop) — the card pin's override loop, lifted out of that test's body and corrected. The property is a fourth argument and the filter declarations(other.body, prop).length > 0 runs INSIDE, because the card pin's existing /overflow-wrap\s*:/ filter is what makes the comment above it true — a rule that cannot override the card classes does not turn the suite red. Take the property away and you get one of two failures: drop the filter and a narrow-viewport padding tweak on a pinned selector turns the suite red for a declaration that cannot change the property, re-breaking a tolerance #71 added on purpose; or hardcode overflow-wrap inside and the non-wrap pins get a check that can never fire. pinned is the rule or the SET of rules the calling pin has already asserted on, and every member is exempt — without the exemption the fix itself would be reported as an override of itself. A conflict is reported for any rule other than the pinned set, at ANY source index, top-level or nested, declaring prop on a comma-split selector part equal to a member of selectors. Symmetric in source order, because an override authored above the pinned rule wins at narrow viewports exactly as one below does. The nested half is the fix for review finding 3 and is M4. THE SELECTOR LOOKUP MUST ANCHOR ON THE SELECTOR'S END — compare a comma-split part to the pinned selector with ===, never selector.includes(pinnedSelector). '.opportunity-roww' and '.tenant-names' both contain their pinned selector as a substring; the current \s*\{ anchors give the pins their rename protection today, and a substring lookup deletes it across all eight pins at once, invisibly. M14 is the GREEN that proves it survives. WHERE THE CONFLICT CHECK IS CALLED, and this is the design decision that matters most. Call it at the card pin and at the new .awaiting-list pin ONLY. The #main > *, .table-scroll, .approval-actions, .approval-actions input, .journal-drawer-body and .tenant-name pins each already collect EVERY rule matching their selector — top-level and nested, per R3 — and assert the property on every one of them, so their every-match loop IS that selector's override check, and it is stronger than a same-selector conflict check because it also catches a rule declaring the WRONG value. Because the helper exempts the pinned set, and on those six the pinned set is every rule that could ever match, a call there could never fire: dead code that reads as coverage. Put one comment line in each of those six tests saying the every-match loop is that selector's override check, so the absence reads as a decision. The distinction is pinned by contract case C10 so it cannot rot silently. THE CARD PIN KEEPS ITS OWN PRE-FILTER — the one place a migration could false-red on a correct stylesheet. Today the card pin builds its candidate set, filters it with /overflow-wrap\s*:/.test(rule.body), and only then calls .find(). That filter is load-bearing: without it find() returns the border / padding / display rule carrying two of the four card classes, with no overflow-wrap at all, and both the selector-set equality assertion against CARD_CLASSES and the deepEqual(values, ['anywhere']) assertion go RED on the shipped file. This pre-filter is DISTINCT from the one inside conflictingOverrides, and both survive the migration. It is named in AC-6 so nobody simplifies it away. THE NEW .awaiting-list PIN, in the house style of #main > * and .tenant-name rather than a whole-body assertion, and in ONE test. In order: (a) collect every rule that is NOT nested, whose comma-split selector part is .awaiting-list or .awaiting-list li, and whose body DECLARES overflow-wrap — the property filter is part of the COLLECTION predicate, not only inside the helper, and the test's own comment must say that in those terms, because a rule added at M5 inside a media query has a selector part that IS exactly .awaiting-list li and an unfiltered collection takes it in, at which point the value assertion fails and the suite goes red for a fix that was never the defect; (b) require the collection NON-EMPTY, with a message that says so, so deleting the declaration and leaving a comment is red (M1), and today's .awaiting-list li rule has zero overflow-wrap declarations in it, so (b) is what turns the current state red rather than vacuous; (c) require each collected rule's overflow-wrap values to deepEqual ['anywhere']; (d) run conflictingOverrides(rules, collected, ['.awaiting-list', '.awaiting-list li', '.awaiting-list li strong', '.awaiting-list li span'], 'overflow-wrap') and require it to report nothing, under R6's watch-list policy. TWO STRICTNESSES WITH THEIR COSTS RECORDED. First, the descendant entries in (d) are a snapshot of the awaiting li's element children — the markup was rendered rather than assumed, and it emits exactly dec_seed_awaiting_1 and one , with no other element child — and they are not an exhaustive set: a third element child carrying free text is invisible to the conflict check with a green suite, which is the descendant hole (M7, M8) in the list rather than in the descendant. validated_work_order.debate_summary:
The critique returned "flawed" with seven findings against v13 — one blocking, three major, four minor — and it is right about the diagnosis and about all three of the findings I re-ran. I upheld the blocking finding and all three majors, took three of the four minors in a lighter or corrected form, and DISMISSED one outright as a path no ticket may change. The disagreement that survives this round is the one that has survived three: whether a four-helper migration belongs in a ticket whose product fix is one declaration.

THE BLOCKING ONE IS A NUMBER, AGAIN, IN THE CRITERION THAT EXISTS TO CATCH A SIDE EFFECT. AC-13 says its grep returns "exactly two hits, the pre-existing ones at 1612 and 1615". It returns six — 216, 404, 406, 408, 1612, 1615 — and the two it names are pre-insertion ordinates that the four helpers, which files[](1)(1) puts beside H1_HOOK at line 23 and mainOf at line 37, move before the grep is ever run. Confirmed by running it. This is the fifth round in a row in which something a reviewer had to disprove was a number rather than a design, and it is in the one criterion added specifically to guard a self-referential insertion, which makes it the most embarrassing place for it to happen. I have not merely corrected it. I looked at the pin the criterion is about and found that the critique also got it slightly wrong in a way that matters: source.split('\n').find(line => line.includes('the h1 carries the page-title hook')) returns the FIRST match, which is 216 — the assert.match(html, H1_HOOK, ...) call inside the H1_HOOK test — not 1612, which is the pin's own find call. So the pin asserts doesNotMatch(/class="page-title"/) against the assertion line itself, and AC-13's own description of the mechanism was wrong as well as its count. The critique's fix — keep a count, say "six before, six after" — restores the exact instrument the previous rejection was about: a number that breaks under the very edit it is meant to survive. I substituted a shape check with no number in it. The first line containing the phrase must be the assert.match(html, H1_HOOK, line, and the set of lines matching either string must be the six pre-existing ones. I confirmed the before state already satisfies both. That survives any comment an implementer writes, any length of block, and the helpers shifting every ordinate below line 37.

THE SECOND MAJOR IS THE ONE THAT WOULD HAVE MADE A DELETED RULE PASS, AND IT IS THE ONLY CHANGE IN THE ORDER THAT TURNS A CURRENTLY-RED MUTATION GREEN. Every other addition here closes a hole; this one opens one. R2 converts the `.page-title` pin from first-match exec to a collection and asserts the three properties "on each", and the assert.ok(rule, 'src/web/styles.css defines a .page-title rule') that today is the only thing reddens a deleted rule goes with it — forEach over an empty collection is vacuously true. I removed the rule from a scratch copy and measured the before state myself: 70 pass / 2 fail, test 65 red, restored byte-identically. The critique is right that the omission is conspicuous rather than principled, since the same order puts "requires the collection NON-EMPTY" in the new pin twice and in R5 twice. Upheld whole, and made structural rather than textual: the guard is a separate numbered clause of AC-6(v), the approach states it, and M21 is a row of its own, because an existing row set with M13 for appending and none for deleting could not have caught it.

THE THIRD MAJOR IS A STRING THE HELPER REJECTS. AC-8(e) says the render half "renders /journal?state=partial", and renderPage guards on ROUTES.includes(route) over five bare paths and throws on anything carrying a query string. The file's own idiom is renderPage('/journal', { override: 'partial' }), which the adjacent table-scroll test already uses. So the only new pin in the ticket, written exactly as the criterion specifies, throws. Confirmed by reading the guard; the critique also executed both forms. Upheld. The browser URL in AC-2 and qa_script step 3 is a different thing and stays as it is, and the criterion now says so in terms, so the next reader does not transpose them.

THE FOURTH MAJOR I PARTLY DISAGREE WITH, AND THE PART I TOOK IS THE WEAKER CLAUSE. AC-2 asserted that "every .table-scroll region still satisfies scrollWidth > clientWidth" across five routes. That sentence is inherited from .sdlc/memory/patterns/phone-width-horizontal-overflow.md, where it is a canary for a wrap rule that LEAKED onto a table — a different claim from "every table is wide", and one that false-reds on a table that legitimately fits its region, which is neither a leak nor a defect. Neither the proposer nor the critic has measured the six-plus tables on those routes and neither can, here. I upheld the substance and restated the clause in the direction the canary actually guards: no .table-scroll region that overflows without the change stops overflowing with it. A leaked wrap rule collapses a wide table's scrollWidth to its clientWidth, which is exactly that direction, so the canary keeps all of its value and loses the unmeasured absolute — and it is checkable in one boot, because the product fix is a single declaration QA can revert, measure and restore. What I did not do is adopt the critique's preferred wording verbatim, which would have required QA to establish a baseline it has no way to establish.

THE MINOR FINDINGS: THREE TAKEN, ONE DISMISSED. Taken in its lighter form: the descendant list in AC-8(d) reports .awaiting-list li span { overflow-wrap: anywhere; } — the same inherited fix M6 accepts on the parent — as a conflict, with neither a policy nor a row. I took the second of the two responses offered and kept the list, because dropping it converts the conflict check into a same-selector check, which the collection predicate already is, and deletes the M7 case the pin exists for. R6 now says the descendant entries are a watch list rather than an allow list, M6b names the RED verdict and its reason, and qa_script step 5 demonstrates it and reverts it. Taken: qa_script step 6 said the rows whose verdicts are specifications are five, while unknowns[0] said most of them are. The helpers do not exist in this tree, so every one of the twenty-three rows is a specification; M12 is the partial exception and it ran against the unmodified tree before the migration. The step now says the budget is twenty-three runs and says which row is the partial exception — the earlier version understated the manual work by a factor of four, in the one place a human reads to decide what they are signing up for. Taken, and in the form the critique called second-best: AC-3 said "by title" and named no titles, so the clause was satisfied by description. Both titles are now pinned verbatim. DISMISSED: that files[] should add .sdlc/memory/patterns/phone-width-horizontal-overflow.md so its mutation list covers the new pin. .sdlc/memory/** is the Librarian's and no ticket may change it — the guard refuses the whole plan for one of them, not for the offending edit — so applying that finding as filed would have cost this run rather than improved it. The critique's evidence is good and its concern about a stale entry is real, and the entry IS now wrong in two ways it will not be: it describes the override check as catching a LATER rule when the check is symmetric, and it says nothing about a ch-only min-width floor. So the content is in risks, as a hand-off the Librarian discharges on merge, with the note that a reviewer should check the hand-off happened rather than trusting the risk to have been read. ONE MORE I TOOK FROM A DIFFERENT DIRECTION THAN IT WAS FILED. The critique called AC-1's "and that rule is the one already declaring display / gap / border / border-radius / padding" a duplication preference, and offered to delete it. I took the other half of its fix instead, because the clause is not merely unobserved — the old text also claimed that a declaration in a NEW rule with the same selector "fails this criterion as well as the new pin", and that claim is false: the new pin collects on selector-plus-declares-the-property, so a same-selector rule with the right value collects and returns the same GREEN.
